name: Priya Schmidt

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel, with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. Your answers stay confidential; what does your factory day involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the spiral-freezer line and check the first trays before they enter packing. I have a two-year technical diploma and am one of the strongest operators at finding faults, especially a bearing that ices up. I like a clean temperature log; I dislike a manager rushing food past a failed check.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who shares the bills, and how do you use AI?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My husband Ben cleans a museum part-time and our grown children live on their own. We rent, my lead wage is low for this job, we have about three weeks saved and only a few similar plants nearby. I use AI now and then to tidy shift notes, but the calibrated thermometer and signed log decide food safety.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the frozen-food crew that small savings in orders are welcome. Someone still has to check the temperature across the first tray leaving the spiral freezer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I lead the freezer line and can hear an iced bearing before it stops, but my wage is low for that responsibility. My husband Ben cleans a museum part-time, our grown children live apart, and we have about three weeks saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the freezer shift, check the first-tray temperatures and compare my occasional AI notes with the actual log. I would put a small amount from each fresh full wage into savings only after rent, food and heating are covered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious even if AI stays small. An ordinary repair bill could use the money we meant to keep for rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you hear the bearing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The fan makes a dry rattle before the temperature rises. I stop the line and call maintenance rather than send warm food out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does AI do for you now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I sometimes use it to tidy shift notes. I still read the calibrated thermometer and signed log before releasing food.

say: I would defend **first-tray temperature checks** on the freezer line.
I would use **occasional AI notes** beside the signed log.
think: Our **three-week reserve** cannot cover a long interruption.
Ben’s **part-time cleaning pay** and my low lead wage leave little slack.
do: Keep **freezer-line leadership** and measure first trays.
Compare **existing AI notes** with signed temperature logs.
Save **small fresh-pay amount** only after essential bills.
feel: **Anxious** about current rent and repair costs.
S0.quote: I stop the line and call maintenance rather than send warm food out.
fieldNote: Her **technical diploma** and strong diagnostic skill exceed what her wage reflects.
The **thin reserve** explains baseline anxiety; new saving uses fresh wages only if essentials permit.

steps.text: Keep leading freezer line and check first-tray temperatures
Save small amount from fresh full wages only after essentials

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say planning software can take office tasks, but robots loading trays into a cold tunnel need a proper guarded trial. I will try a new defrost chart if the maintenance lead has tested it first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A tray robot could reduce my crew’s paid hours even if the freezer still needs a skilled lead. Our three-week reserve and the few similar plants nearby leave little room for a smaller pay packet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for an offered paid training slot using the stopped freezer and recorded old batches, with maintenance supervising the isolated drive. If approved I would learn the new AI defrost schedule against actual temperature logs; after an hours cut I would apply for posted reachable lead roles only where pay after travel covers rent and food.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about the rota but willing to try a chart that has passed a physical test. The freezer has no sympathy for a screen that guessed the wrong temperature.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you alter a live freezer first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. The maintenance lead must isolate the drive and give me a paid practice place before I touch the schedule.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would another plant hire you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There are few local ones. I would need a real posting and a wage that still covers rent after the journey.

I would keep **signed temperature logs** beside any new chart.
think: A tray robot could reduce **my paid crew hours**.
Three **weeks saved** and few nearby plants make cuts serious.
do: Request **offered paid safe practice** on stopped freezer with maintenance.
Learn **new AI defrost schedule** only against recorded temperatures.
Apply after **hour cuts** for posted reachable bill-covering net-pay lead work.
feel: **Anxious** about plausible cuts to her own wage.
S1.quote: The freezer has no sympathy for a screen that guessed the wrong temperature.
fieldNote: Her **steady AI use** supports learning a new chart only through offered supervised paid safe practice.
Any **job application** needs actual cuts, a reachable posting and net pay after travel covering essentials.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking AGI in 2028 finds me sixty, and capable food-handling robots around 2031 find me sixty-three. The office roster changes first, then the tray loaders could change the whole line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect management to close my freezer shift once robots can load and inspect trays. Ben’s cleaning hours and three weeks saved cannot cover rent for long, and I lie awake over the next heating bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for written closure and severance terms and cancel the planned visit to our daughter. I would apply for posted reachable food-line or cold-store jobs with bill-covering net pay after travel before leaving, and ask the housing office about available help if the shift ends without an adequate offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be alarmed about losing a large part of our wages. A temperature log cannot warm the flat if the shift disappears.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retire at sixty-three?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if verified retirement income and Ben’s confirmed pay cover housing, food and health costs. We have no figures that show that, so I expect to keep earning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could your daughter pay instead?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She has her own bills. I might ask for a ride to an interview, not put her wages into our budget.

say: I would demand **written closure terms** before capable robots arrive.
I would ask for **actual severance figures** instead of reassurance.
think: I expect **my freezer shift** to close around 2031.
Three **weeks saved** and part-time pay cannot cover rent.
do: Request **written freezer staffing terms** and severance.
Cancel **planned daughter visit** to protect rent money.
Apply for **posted reachable jobs** at bill-covering net pay before leaving.
feel: **Alarmed** and losing sleep over expected major wage loss.
S2.quote: A temperature log cannot warm the flat if the shift disappears.
fieldNote: Expected **shift closure** supports alarm despite high skill and a partner earning.
The **job path** needs posted reachable work, adequate net pay and a real offer before resignation.

steps.text: Request written freezer staffing and severance terms
Cancel planned daughter visit to protect rent money
Apply for posted reachable bill-covering net-pay food or cold-store job before leaving
Ask housing office about available help if shift ends without adequate offer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking AGI in 2031 finds me sixty-three, and capable tray robots around 2034 find me sixty-six. Five years is enough to offer real refrigeration-maintenance training if the factory means it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My technical diploma and fault-finding would help, but refrigerant work needs its own recognised qualification and safe supervised practice. Unpaid course days would take rent money, and a certificate with no reachable paid job would be useless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the paid freezer shift and ask for a funded course during paid hours. If offered an actual place with an isolated system and a qualified refrigeration fitter supervising, plus a posted reachable job whose pay after travel covers rent and food, I would enrol; after qualifying I would apply for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about our thin cash cushion even with more warning. I want to learn beside a cold, isolated pipe, not a leaking one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you practise?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The fitter would isolate the cooling circuit and supervise a test on a training unit. I would not open a live refrigerant line to prove my nerve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If no course opens?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep paid shifts and compare posted cold-store jobs after hour cuts. I would not buy private training out of three weeks saved.

say: I would ask for **paid refrigeration training** before later robots.
I would require **posted local wages** before course enrolment.
think: My **fault-finding skill** helps but is not a refrigeration licence.
An **unpaid course** would use rent money before any offer.
do: Enrol in **funded refrigeration course** only with offered paid safe practice and adequate posted job.
Apply after **qualification** for posted reachable bill-covering net-pay refrigeration work.
feel: **Anxious** about thin savings, open to proven practical training.
S3.quote: I want to learn beside a cold, isolated pipe, not a leaking one.
fieldNote: Her **high existing skill** does not replace a required refrigerant qualification.
The **later application** needs offered funded paid safe practice and a posted reachable adequate job.

steps.text: Keep paid spiral-freezer shifts while available
Enrol if offered funded paid isolated refrigeration place and adequate posted job
Apply after qualification for posted reachable bill-covering net-pay refrigeration role
Search posted cold-store jobs after cuts if no course place opens

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking AGI in 2036 finds me sixty-eight, and capable tray robots around 2039 find me seventy-one. Ten years lets Ben and me see whether our retirement figures can cover the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I had hoped to finish full-time factory work at sixty-seven, but three weeks saved will not fund years without a wage. I do not know what any pension pays, and Ben’s future cleaning hours cannot be assumed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now in 2026 I would keep the freezer shift and save a little from fresh full wages only after rent, food and heat. I would request retirement and rent figures; if verified household income covers housing, food and health costs at sixty-seven I would stop factory work then, otherwise continue safe paid work, and after 2036 compare posted reachable bill-covering jobs only if still employed and my hours fell.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious even with a decade because this winter’s rent and heat still have dates. I will not give notice on a retirement figure I have not seen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the figures are short?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep safe paid work and compare real wages after travel if shifts fell. I cannot stop because the calendar says sixty-seven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your children contribute?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They have households of their own. A lift to an appointment is help; a standing payment is not our plan.

I would separate **2036 AGI** from 2039 tray robots.

feel: **Anxious** because present rent and heat keep the reserve thin.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because tray robots around 2031 could close my freezer shift while rent and heat are due. Written staffing terms, offered funded paid safe refrigeration training and posted reachable work with enough pay after travel would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who signed the temperature sheet before the first tray left the freezer. A warm tray has a cost that no tidy note can erase.

headlineQuote: A warm tray has a cost that no tidy note can erase.
portrait: **Priya**, 58, leads a spiral freezer with a two-year technical diploma and among the strongest fault-finding skills at the plant.
Her **low lead pay**, part-time museum-cleaner husband Ben, grown children, rent, three-week reserve and few nearby plants create pressure.
She uses **AI occasionally** and would learn a new defrost chart only through offered paid safe practice.
Expected **2031 shift closure** alarms her; a planned age-sixty-seven exit needs verified household income.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries her most because 2031 tray robots may close her paid freezer shift while rent remains.
whatWouldHelp: Written **staffing terms**, offered funded paid safe training and posted reachable bill-covering net-pay work would help.
